full_judgment: 7. It appears that the learned Judge of the High Court Division refused to interfere with the finding of the lower appellate Court that the applications for pre-emption were not barred by limitation but the learned Judge reversed the decision of the lower appellate Court on the ground that it was wrongly held by the said Court that the pre-emptors had locus standi to file the applications for pre-emption. The learned Judge observed that the lower appellate Court had committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record by failing to appreciate the burden of proof in the present case. The preempted-respondents positively stated in their written objection that the pre-emptors had sold out all their shares in the case holding and they had no locus standi to prefer the application for pre-emption. The learned Judge observed that pre-emptor No. 1 deposing as PW 1 completely yielded to the assertion of the preempted-respondents in his cross-examination and therefore, they (the pre-empties) had no further burden to prove that the pre-emptors had sold out all their shares in the case holding. The burden of proof lay with the pre-emptors to prove that they still retained some shares in the case Khatian in order to be able to ask for pre-emption as co-sharers. The learned Judge further observed that the lower appellate Court had misread the evidence of PW 1 in that the witness never stated that he was an existing co-sharer in the case Khatian, but he merely stated that it was not a fact that he was not a co-sharer. This was an expression of opinion as to his status in the case holding and not a statement of fact, the learned Judge held. It was finally held that the trial Court had correctly found that the pre-emptors had disqualified themselves by making a blatant admission that they had sold out all their (share of) lands in the case Khatian.
